## Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

- Follow an email from the sender's mail program to the recipient's
  mailbox, and name the protocol and the port of each step.
- Find the mail servers of a domain and its sending policy in the DNS,
  with `dig`.
- Tell the **envelope** of an email (SMTP commands) from its
  **message** (headers and body), and explain why that makes spoofing
  easy.
- Explain what a mock server is, and run Mailpit with Docker Compose.
- Open a TCP connection with `ncat`, as a client and as a server, and
  send an email by hand.
- Read the code of a small Java SMTP client, and relate each line to
  the commands you typed.

SMTP is the worked example of [chapter 06](06-application-protocols.qmd):
here you talk to a real server, by hand, then with a program. In
[practical work 2](../practical-work/pw2.qmd) you do the same with your
own protocol.

## A quick reminder about networking

### IP addresses

Each machine connected to the Internet has an **IP address**, which
identifies it on the network. IPv4 addresses (`193.134.223.20`) are
32-bit numbers, and there are not enough of them for every device.
**NAT** (Network Address Translation) routers let several machines
share one public address: your home router does this for all your
devices. **IPv6**, with 128-bit addresses (`2001:db8::1`), was created
to solve the shortage.

### Names and the DNS

People use names, programs need addresses. The **DNS** (Domain Name
System) translates one into the other. `nslookup` asks it for the
address of a name:

```sh
nslookup heig-vd.ch
```

```text
Server:         172.20.10.1
Address:        172.20.10.1#53

Non-authoritative answer:
Name:   heig-vd.ch
Address: 193.134.223.20
```

`Server` is the DNS server that answered, the one your network gave you;
yours will differ. `Address` is the answer. When you open a web page,
your browser does the same lookup first, then connects to that
address. The DNS holds more than addresses, as you will see for mail
below.

### Port numbers

An **IP address** identifies a machine; a **port** identifies a
program on that machine. Think of a street address and an apartment
number. A port is a 16-bit number, from 0 to 65535. TCP and UDP each
have their own ports: TCP port 53 and UDP port 53 are two different
ports, which two different programs can use. The ranges ([chapter 06](06-application-protocols.qmd#port)) and
some well-known examples:

| Range | Examples |
|---|---|
| 0-1023, system (well-known) ports | 20, 21 FTP · 22 SSH · 23 Telnet · 25, 465, 587 SMTP · 53 DNS · 80, 443 HTTP, HTTPS · 110, 995 POP3 · 123 NTP · 143, 993 IMAP |
| 1024-49151, user (registered) ports | 3306 MySQL · 5432 PostgreSQL · 6379 Redis · 8080 HTTP (alternative) · 25565 Minecraft · 27017 MongoDB |
| 49152-65535, dynamic ports | Never registered; used for temporary connections and private services, such as 51820 WireGuard and 64738 Mumble |

On Linux and macOS, listening on a port below 1024 usually needs special
rights. Wikipedia keeps a
[list of TCP and UDP port numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_TCP_and_UDP_port_numbers).

## How an email travels

Bob writes to `alice@gmail.com` from his company address and clicks
**Send**. Four kinds of programs take part:

| Program | Role | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **MUA**, Mail User Agent | The mail program of a person: writes, sends, reads | Thunderbird, Outlook, Apple Mail, the Gmail web page |
| **MSA**, Mail Submission Agent | Accepts the mails of its own users, usually after they log in | The "outgoing server" of a mail account |
| **MTA**, Mail Transfer Agent | Carries mails from server to server, to the domain of the recipient | Microsoft Exchange, Postfix, Gmail's servers |
| **Mailbox** | Stores the mails of a user until the MUA fetches them | On the server of the recipient |

The MSA and the MTA are often the same server program, with two roles.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    B["Bob's MUA"] -- "SMTP, port 587 or 465" --> MSA["Bob's server<br>(MSA, then MTA)"]
    MSA -- "DNS: MX of gmail.com?" --> DNS[(DNS)]
    MSA -- "SMTP, port 25" --> MTA["Alice's server<br>(MTA, mailbox)"]
    MTA -- "IMAP or POP3" --> A["Alice's MUA"]
```

1. Bob's MUA **submits** the mail to his MSA with SMTP. Bob logs in
   first: the MSA usually accepts mails only from its own users.
2. Bob's MTA asks the DNS which servers receive the mail of
   `gmail.com` (the **MX** records, see below).
3. It **relays** the mail with SMTP to one of these servers, on port
   25. Alice's server stores it in her mailbox.
4. Alice's MUA fetches the mail with **IMAP** or **POP3**.

The same route, with the SMTP commands of each step:

```{mermaid}
sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Bob's MUA (Outlook)
    participant S1 as Bob's server (MS Exchange)
    participant S2 as Alice's server (Gmail)
    participant A as Alice's MUA (Thunderbird)
    B->>S1: connect, EHLO
    B->>S1: MAIL FROM, RCPT TO
    B->>S1: DATA, then the message
    B->>S1: QUIT
    Note over S1: stores the mail, finds Alice's server (MX)
    S1->>S2: connect, EHLO
    S1->>S2: MAIL FROM, RCPT TO
    S1->>S2: DATA, then the message
    S1->>S2: QUIT
    Note over S2: stores the mail in Alice's mailbox
    A->>S2: fetches the mail (IMAP or POP3)
```

SMTP only **sends**: it pushes a mail one step further, up to the
mailbox. Reading the mailbox is the job of two other protocols:

- **POP3** downloads the mails, and can delete them from the
  server. Simple, made for one device.
- **IMAP** keeps the mails on the server and **synchronizes** the
  devices: a mail read on the phone is marked as read on the laptop
  too, and folders exist on the server. This is what MUAs use today.

A webmail such as the Gmail web page is a MUA running on the server:
your browser talks HTTP to it, and it reads the mailbox for you,
often with IMAP.

### Ports

| Protocol | Use | Plain text | TLS from the start |
|---|---|---|---|
| SMTP | Relay between MTAs | 25 | |
| SMTP | Submission by a MUA | 587, then `STARTTLS` | 465 |
| POP3 | Reading | 110 | 995 |
| IMAP | Reading | 143 | 993 |

On 587, the connection starts in clear text, and the client sends
`STARTTLS` to switch to TLS before anything private (a password, the
mail) is sent; on 465, 995 and 993, TLS starts at once. This is why
`ncat` can talk to ports 25 and 587 only.

## Mail and the DNS

Besides addresses, the DNS gives the mail servers of a domain, and
more. It stores **records**, each with a type:

| Type | Gives | Example for `heig-vd.ch` |
|---|---|---|
| `A` | An IPv4 address | `193.134.223.20` |
| `AAAA` | An IPv6 address | |
| `CNAME` | An alias: "this name is another name" | |
| `NS` | The DNS servers responsible for the domain | |
| `MX` | The servers that receive the mail of the domain | `0 heigvd-ch01b.mail.protection.outlook.com.` |
| `TXT` | Free text, used for policies such as SPF | `v=spf1 ... -all` |

`dig` asks the DNS for one type of record. `+short` keeps only the
answer:

```sh
dig +short heig-vd.ch MX
```

```text
0 heigvd-ch01b.mail.protection.outlook.com.
```

The mail of HEIG-VD is received by Microsoft's servers. The `0` before
the name is the **preference**: when a domain has several MX records,
the MTA tries the lowest number first.

`dig` is part of macOS. On Ubuntu and in WSL, install it with
`sudo apt install bind9-dnsutils` if `dig` is missing. On Windows,
`nslookup -type=mx heig-vd.ch` gives the same answer in another layout.

## Envelope and message

An SMTP transaction carries two different things.

The **envelope** is made of SMTP commands. It tells the servers where
to deliver the mail:

- `MAIL FROM:<...>`: where to send an error report if the mail cannot
  be delivered (the *return path*);
- `RCPT TO:<...>`: one command per recipient. The servers deliver
  according to these addresses, never according to the `To:` or `Cc:`
  headers.

The **message** is what follows `DATA`. Its format is defined by
[RFC 5322](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5322), separate from SMTP:

```text
From: Alice <alice@example.com>
To: Bob <bob@example.com>
Subject: Hello from ncat

Hi Bob,
this mail was typed by hand.
```

- **Headers** first, one per line, `Name: value`. A long header
  continues on the next lines, which start with a space. `From`, `To`, `Cc`,
  `Subject` and `Date` are the ones the MUA displays.
- An **empty line** separates the headers from the body.
- The **body** is the text of the mail.

The servers deliver to the envelope; the MUA displays the headers.
Nothing in SMTP checks that the two match: the `From:` header can show
any address, and SMTP itself checks neither `From:` nor `MAIL FROM`.
The mechanism below was added for that.

## Spam, spoofing and the policies against them

SMTP was designed in 1982, for a network where the machines trusted
each other. Out of the box, it has no authentication and no encryption,
and any server can claim to send for any domain. Writing a fake `From:`
header is called **spoofing**, and it is how phishing mails pretend to
come from your bank or from the school.

**SPF** ([RFC 7208](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7208)) was added
later: a domain publishes in a `TXT` record of the DNS the IP addresses
allowed to send mail for it (for the domain of `MAIL FROM`). The
receiving server checks the address of the sender, and decides to
accept, reject, or mark the mail as spam. Two other mechanisms complete
it, DKIM and DMARC (*Go further*).

The SPF record of HEIG-VD:

```sh
dig +short heig-vd.ch TXT
```

```text
"v=spf1 ip4:193.134.218.124 ip4:145.232.233.54 ip4:185.144.39.35/32 ip4:185.144.39.39/32  include:spf.protection.outlook.com include:spf.hefr.ch include:_spf.createsend.com include:c2qslai37u.powerspf.com -all"
```

(other `TXT` records of the domain, which prove ownership to various
services, are left out here)

- `v=spf1` says that this `TXT` record is an SPF policy.
- `ip4:...` gives an address allowed to send.
- `include:...` allows the addresses listed in the SPF record of
  another domain too, here Microsoft's servers and those of a
  newsletter service.
- `-all` makes every other address fail. `~all` would mean "probably
  not allowed, accept but mark as suspect".

Running your own mail server takes work: if spammers use it, its IP
address lands on **blocklists**, and the other servers refuse its mail.
This is why most companies and schools let Microsoft or Google run
theirs.

::: {.callout-warning}
Spoofing an address takes a few lines. Sending mails
under someone else's name, or to people who did not ask for them, is
forbidden by the rules of HEIG-VD and can be illegal. Send your test
mails to Mailpit only.
:::

## Mock servers

A program that sends mails needs a server to test against. A real one
is the wrong choice: a bug in a loop can send thousands of mails to
real people, get your address blocked, or look like an attack.

A **mock server** imitates a real server for testing. It speaks the
same protocol, but delivers nothing, and shows you what it received.
The same idea exists for databases, web APIs, payment services.

[Mailpit](https://mailpit.axllent.org/) is a mock SMTP server. It
accepts every mail, keeps it in a temporary database, and shows it in a web
interface. Its `compose.yaml`, in the code examples:

```yaml
services:
  mailpit:
    image: axllent/mailpit:v1.32
    ports:
      # SMTP server, on Mailpit's default port
      - 1025:1025
      # Web interface: http://localhost:8025
      - 8025:8025
```

It listens for SMTP on port 1025, the web interface is on
<http://localhost:8025>.

## ncat

[ncat](https://nmap.org/ncat/) opens a TCP (or UDP) connection, sends
what you type, and prints what it receives. It has no protocol of its
own. The protocol is you. It is the tool to test a text protocol by
hand, to check that a server answers, or to see exactly what a client
sends.

Install it:

| System | Command |
|---|---|
| Ubuntu, WSL | `sudo apt install ncat` |
| macOS | `brew install nmap` (ncat is part of nmap) |

Then check:

```sh
ncat --version
```

```text
Ncat: Version 7.94SVN ( https://nmap.org/ncat )
```

The version differs between systems (7.98 with Homebrew); any recent
one works.

The two modes you need:

```sh
# Client: connect to port 1025 of localhost
ncat -C localhost 1025

# Server: listen on port 2525, and print what the client sends
ncat -l -C 2525
```

`-C` sends each line you type with `\r\n` (CR LF) at the end, instead
of the `\n` your terminal produces. SMTP requires CR LF. Some servers
accept a plain `\n` for commands, but the end of the mail must be
exactly `\r\n.\r\n`: without `-C`, the `.` is just one more line of
text, and the server waits for the real end until its timeout closes
the connection, 5 minutes later in Mailpit ([exercise 2](#sec-ex2)
shows it).

ncat stops by itself when the other side closes the connection. To
leave earlier, press `Ctrl` + `C`.

`nc` (netcat) and `telnet` do the same job and are installed on many
systems; their options differ from ncat's (`telnet` always sends CR LF,
`nc` has `-c` or `-C` depending on the version).

## Sending an email by hand

Start Mailpit, from the directory `07-smtp-and-ncat` of the
[code examples]({{< var examples-url >}}):

```sh
cd dai-code-examples
git pull
cd 07-smtp-and-ncat
docker compose up -d
```

Open <http://localhost:8025> in a browser: the inbox is empty. In a
second terminal, follow the log of the server:

```sh
docker compose logs -f
```

```text
mailpit-1  | time="2026/10/27 06:26:17" level=info msg="[smtpd] starting on [::]:1025 (no encryption)"
mailpit-1  | time="2026/10/27 06:26:17" level=warning msg="[http] listening on [::]:8025 without --ui-auth-file or --allowed-hosts; the API is reachable from any host that can route to this interface"
mailpit-1  | time="2026/10/27 06:26:17" level=info msg="[http] starting on [::]:8025"
mailpit-1  | time="2026/10/27 06:26:17" level=info msg="[http] accessible via http://localhost:8025/"
```

`-f` keeps the log open and shows new lines as they come. Mailpit logs
each **error** it answers, such as
`[smtpd] response (192.168.65.1) 503 5.5.1 Bad sequence of commands`,
but not the mails it accepts: those appear in the web interface. When a
command fails, the log tells you what the server understood. The
warning says that the web interface has no password, which is fine for
tests on your own machine. `Ctrl` + `C` stops following the log;
Mailpit keeps running.

In a third terminal, connect:

```sh
ncat -C localhost 1025
```

Then type the lines marked `C:` (without `C:`); the lines `S:` are the
answers of the server. Wait for each answer before typing the next
command.

```text
S: 220 a825881dcf8e Mailpit ESMTP Service ready
C: EHLO my-laptop.local
S: 250-a825881dcf8e greets my-laptop.local
S: 250-SIZE 52428800
S: 250-ENHANCEDSTATUSCODES
S: 250-8BITMIME
S: 250 SMTPUTF8
C: MAIL FROM:<alice@example.com>
S: 250 2.1.0 Ok
C: RCPT TO:<bob@example.com>
S: 250 2.1.5 Ok
C: DATA
S: 354 Start mail input; end with <CR><LF>.<CR><LF>
C: From: Alice <alice@example.com>
C: To: Bob <bob@example.com>
C: Subject: Hello from ncat
C:
C: Hi Bob,
C: this mail was typed by hand.
C: .
S: 250 2.0.0 Ok: queued as 0WN74Fza0O8ED2H17pjg9l
C: QUIT
S: 221 2.0.0 a825881dcf8e Mailpit ESMTP Service closing transmission channel
```

The mail is in the web interface. Step by step:

| Command | Meaning | Success |
|---|---|---|
| (connection) | The server speaks first | `220` |
| `EHLO <name of your machine>` | Hello; the answer lists the extensions of the server | `250`, several lines |
| `MAIL FROM:<address>` | Starts a mail, gives the return path | `250` |
| `RCPT TO:<address>` | One recipient; repeat for each | `250` |
| `DATA` | The message follows | `354` |
| headers, empty line, body, `.` | The message, ended by a line holding a single `.` | `250` |
| `QUIT` | Goodbye; the server closes the connection | `221` |

What [chapter 06](06-application-protocols.qmd) said about SMTP is
all here:

- The **first digit** of a code is what a program tests: `2` success,
  `3` go on (send the data), `4` temporary failure (try again later),
  `5` permanent failure.
- A reply takes several lines when the code is followed by `-`
  (`250-`); the line with a space (`250 `) is the last one.
- Codes such as `2.1.0` after the main code are *enhanced status
  codes*, announced by `ENHANCEDSTATUSCODES` in the `EHLO` answer; they
  give more detail.
- `HELO` is the older form of `EHLO`, without the list of extensions.

A command in the wrong place gets an error, and the connection stays
open; the error also appears in Mailpit's log:

```text
C: RCPT TO:<bob@example.com>
S: 503 5.5.1 Bad sequence of commands (MAIL required before RCPT)
```

The `<>` around the addresses are part of the syntax: without them,
the server answers with an error too.

When you are done, stop Mailpit; it forgets the mails:

```sh
docker compose down
```

## A Java SMTP client

`SmtpClient.java`, in the same directory, sends the same mail with the
same commands. It uses a `Socket` (`java.net`): a TCP connection,
with an input stream and an output stream. You will see sockets in
detail in the TCP & UDP chapter. Here, look at what goes around them:
the readers and writers of [chapter 04](04-java-io.qmd).

```java
try (Socket socket = new Socket(host, port);
    BufferedReader in =
        new BufferedReader(
            new InputStreamReader(socket.getInputStream(), StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
    BufferedWriter out =
        new BufferedWriter(
            new OutputStreamWriter(socket.getOutputStream(), StandardCharsets.UTF_8))) {

  // The server speaks first
  expect(in, 220);

  send(out, "EHLO my-laptop.local");
  expect(in, 250);
  // ...
```

Two small methods do the work:

```java
/** Sends one line, ended by CRLF. */
private static void send(BufferedWriter out, String line) throws IOException {
  System.out.println("C: " + line);
  out.write(line + "\r\n");
  out.flush();
}

/** Reads a whole reply and checks its code. Lines "250-..." announce that more lines follow. */
private static void expect(BufferedReader in, int code) throws IOException {
  String line;
  do {
    line = in.readLine();
    if (line == null) {
      throw new IOException("The server closed the connection");
    }
    System.out.println("S: " + line);
  } while (line.length() > 3 && line.charAt(3) == '-');

  if (!line.startsWith(code + "")) {
    throw new IOException("Expected " + code + ", received: " + line);
  }
}
```

- `send` writes `\r\n` itself: `BufferedWriter.newLine()` would write
  the line separator of the system, `\n` on Linux and macOS.
- `flush()` sends the line now. Without it, the line stays in the
  buffer, the server waits for it, the client waits for the answer, and
  both wait until a timeout closes the connection.
- `expect` reads lines until the last line of the reply, the one
  without `-`. Then the next answer read belongs to the next command.
- `readLine()` returns `null` when the server closes the connection:
  the end of the stream.

Run it with Mailpit started:

```sh
java SmtpClient.java
```

It prints the whole exchange, in the same format as above, and the
mail appears in Mailpit. `java SmtpClient.java <host> <port>` connects
elsewhere.

## Exercises

Start Mailpit for the exercises (`docker compose up -d` in
`07-smtp-and-ncat`), and stop it at the end.

### Exercise 1: Send an email by hand {#sec-ex1}

Send a mail to Mailpit with ncat, as in the chapter, with your own
text. Then, in the web interface, open the mail and look at its
headers (**Headers** tab, or **Raw**). Which ones did you write? Which
ones were added, and by whom?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
You wrote `From`, `To`, `Subject`. Mailpit added `Received:` (its
name, your `EHLO` name, the date), `Return-Path:` (the address of
`MAIL FROM`) and a `Message-ID:` because the message had none. A real
MUA writes `Date` and `Message-ID` itself. Each server on the way adds
its own `Received:` line at the top, so the headers of a mail tell its
route, newest first.
:::

### Exercise 2: Forget `-C` {#sec-ex2}

Connect **without** `-C`: `ncat localhost 1025`. Send a whole mail.

1. Do the commands work?
2. What happens after the `.`? Type `QUIT`. Then explain.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
1. Yes: Mailpit accepts commands that end with `\n` alone.
2. Nothing: the server does not answer, and `QUIT` gets no answer
   either. The end of the mail is `\r\n.\r\n`, and ncat sent `\n.\n`:
   for the server, the `.` and `QUIT` are lines of the mail. It waits
   for the real end. Press `Ctrl` + `C`; the mail is never delivered.
   If you wait, Mailpit gives up after 5 minutes: it answers `421`
   (timeout exceeded) and closes the connection.
:::

### Exercise 3: Be the server {#sec-ex3}

Play Mailpit's role for the Java client. In one terminal:

```sh
ncat -l -C 2525
```

In a second terminal:

```sh
java SmtpClient.java localhost 2525
```

The client's commands appear in the first terminal. Answer each one,
by hand, with a reply that lets the client go on, until it says
goodbye.

1. Which line do you have to type first? Why does nothing happen until
   you do?
2. Answer `EHLO` with a reply of two lines. What does the client do?
3. Answer `RCPT TO` with `550 No such user`. What happens?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
1. A `220` greeting, such as `220 my fake server`: in SMTP the server
   speaks first, and the client waits for it before sending `EHLO`.
2. With `250-hello` then `250 ok`, the client reads both lines and only
   then sends `MAIL FROM`: `expect` reads until the line without `-`.
3. `expect` throws `IOException: Expected 250, received: 550 No such
   user`, the try-with-resources closes the socket, and ncat stops.
   A real client would go on with the other recipients, or send
   `QUIT`.
:::

### Exercise 4: Improve the client {#sec-ex4}

1. Suppose the client read **one line** after each command. Which
   answer would it read after `MAIL FROM`? What would go wrong
   next? Try it: replace the `do ... while` with a single
   `readLine()`.
2. Let the client send the mail to several recipients, given on the
   command line.
3. Let it read the body of the mail from a text file. Which line of a
   file would break the protocol? Handle it.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
1. After `EHLO`, it read only `250-... greets ...`. After `MAIL FROM`,
   it read the next line of the `EHLO` reply, `250-SIZE ...`: from
   there on, each command was matched with an older answer. All the
   codes were `250`, so nothing showed, until `DATA`:

   ```text
   C: DATA
   S: 250-8BITMIME
   Exception in thread "main" java.io.IOException: Expected 354, received: 250-8BITMIME
   ```

   A client that does not check the codes goes on, and sends the mail
   before the server said `354`. Every reply must be read whole.
2. One `RCPT TO` per address, each followed by `expect(in, 250)`, all
   before `DATA`. Put the addresses you want to show in the `To:`
   header.
3. A line holding a single `.` would end the mail early, and the rest
   of the file would be read as commands. Apply dot-stuffing (*Go
   further*, "A line with a single dot"): before
   sending a line of the body, add a `.` if it starts with `.`
   (`line.startsWith(".") ? "." + line : line`).
:::

## Test your knowledge

- Name the programs a mail goes through from Bob to Alice, and the
  protocol of each step.
- What is the difference between POP3 and IMAP?
- Why does a MUA use port 587 or 465, and an MTA port 25?
- Which DNS record tells where to deliver the mail of a domain? What
  does the number before the name mean?
- What is the difference between `RCPT TO` and the `To:` header?
- What does SPF check?
- What is a mock server? Why do you test an SMTP client against one?
- What does `-C` change in ncat? What breaks without it?
- How does a client know that a reply of the server is complete?

## Go further

Optional content: useful general knowledge, not required for the
evaluations.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="CC, Bcc, HTML and attachments"}
- Are you able to send an email with a CC recipient?
- Are you able to send an email with a BCC recipient?
- Are you able to send an email with HTML content?
- Are you able to send an email with an attachment?

The envelope and the headers explain the first two. The servers
deliver to the `RCPT TO` commands, never to the `To:` or `Cc:`
headers:

- **CC**: one `RCPT TO` per recipient, and a `Cc:` header that lists
  the addresses you choose to show.
- **Bcc**: the sender's MUA adds a `RCPT TO` for the address, and
  leaves it out of the headers. The other recipients cannot see that
  this person received the mail.
- A **mailing list** works the same way: a mail with
  `To: dai@lists.example.com` is sent to each member's own address.

HTML content and attachments need MIME, in the next box.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Accents, HTML and attachments: MIME"}
SMTP was made for lines of ASCII text. **MIME** (RFC 2045 and the
following ones) adds headers that say how the body is encoded:

```text
Subject: =?UTF-8?B?Q2Fmw6kgw6AgWXZlcmRvbg==?=
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
```

The subject is an *encoded word*: `UTF-8`, `B` for Base64, then the
UTF-8 bytes of "Café à Yverdon" in Base64. Mailpit displays it
decoded. A mail with an HTML version and an attachment has the type
`multipart/mixed`: the body is cut into parts, each with its own
headers, separated by a boundary line. MUAs and mail libraries
(Jakarta Mail in Java) write all this for you. Servers that announce
`SMTPUTF8` and `8BITMIME` also accept UTF-8 directly, when the client
asks for it in `MAIL FROM` (`BODY=8BITMIME`, `SMTPUTF8`).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="DKIM and DMARC"}
SPF checks the address of the sending server. Two more mechanisms,
also published in the DNS, complete it:

- **DKIM** ([RFC 6376](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6376)): the
  sending server signs the message; the public key to check the
  signature is in the DNS.
- **DMARC** ([RFC 9989](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9989)): a
  `TXT` record at `_dmarc.<domain>` asks that the `From:` header, the
  one the reader sees, match the domain that SPF or DKIM checked, and
  says what to do with a mail that fails.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="SMTP smuggling"}
In 2023, researchers showed that servers disagreed on the end of a mail:
some accepted `\n.\n` and similar sequences as an end, others only
`\r\n.\r\n`. A sender could
hide a second, spoofed mail inside the text of the first one, and an
outgoing server would pass it on as part of a legitimate mail. The fix
is the rule of exercise 2: only `\r\n.\r\n` ends a mail. Details in the
[original article](https://sec-consult.com/blog/detail/smtp-smuggling-spoofing-e-mails-worldwide/).
:::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Exercise: ask the DNS"}
1. Find the mail servers of `heig-vd.ch`, `gmail.com` and a domain of
   your choice (`proton.me`, `outlook.com`, your previous school).
   Which one does an MTA try first?
2. Find the SPF record of `gmail.com`. What does `redirect=` mean? Find
   the record it points to.
3. Find the DMARC record of `heig-vd.ch` and of `gmail.com`. What do
   they ask for a mail that fails?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
1. `dig +short <domain> MX`. The record with the **lowest** preference
   is tried first: for `gmail.com`, `gmail-smtp-in.l.google.com` (5).
   HEIG-VD has a single record, preference 0.
2. `dig +short gmail.com TXT` gives `v=spf1 redirect=_spf.google.com`:
   the policy of `gmail.com` is the policy of `_spf.google.com`.
   `dig +short _spf.google.com TXT` shows it: a list of `ip4:` and
   `ip6:` ranges, ending with `~all`.
3. `dig +short _dmarc.heig-vd.ch TXT` and
   `dig +short _dmarc.gmail.com TXT`. Both have `p=none`: do nothing
   special with a mail that fails; both ask receivers to send reports
   (`rua=`) to the given address. Gmail adds `sp=quarantine` for its subdomains:
   their failed mails go to spam. `p=reject` would ask to refuse the
   mail.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Exercise: envelope against headers"}
In one SMTP transaction:

- the envelope says `MAIL FROM:<eve@example.com>` and has two
  recipients, `bob@example.com` and `carol@example.com`;
- the headers say `From: The Boss <boss@heig-vd.ch>` and only
  `To: Bob <bob@example.com>`.

Send it, then open it in Mailpit.

1. Which sender does the inbox show? Where does `eve` appear?
2. Carol received the mail. How does Bob know? How does Mailpit show
   her?
3. A real server receives this mail from your laptop. What do SPF and
   DMARC say about it?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
1. The inbox shows **The Boss**, the `From:` header. `eve@example.com`
   is in the `Return-Path:` header, which comes from `MAIL FROM`.
2. Bob cannot know: Carol is in no header. She is a **Bcc** recipient.
   Mailpit adds a `Bcc:` line so that you can see her; a real server
   delivers the mail to her and shows nothing.
3. SPF checks the domain of `MAIL FROM`, `example.com`: your laptop is
   not in its list. DMARC checks the `From:` domain, `heig-vd.ch`: it
   does not match the domain SPF checked, and nothing signed the mail
   with DKIM for `heig-vd.ch`. Both fail. With `p=none`, as HEIG-VD
   publishes today, the receiving server may still deliver the mail,
   often into the spam folder.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="A line with a single dot"}
The text of your mail contains a line with a single `.`. With ncat,
how do you send it so that it stays in the mail? Check in Mailpit.
Find the rule in section 4.5.2 of
[RFC 5321](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5321).

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Type `..`: the client doubles a `.` at the start of any line of text
(*dot-stuffing*), and the server removes the first `.` of each line
that starts with one. A line `..Hello` arrives as `.Hello`, a line
`..` as `.`. Only a line holding a single `.` ends the mail.
:::
::::
